spans.heading: Publicly-funded investment account for babies
spans.text: A 2019 analysis of the proposal by Naomi Zewde projects that baby bonds would reduce the median racial wealth gap between white and black young Americans from a factor of 16 to a factor of 1.4.

spans.heading: Racial wealth gap
spans.text: The racial wealth gap in the United States is well-documented: a 2020 study by Ashman and Neumuller found, based on Survey of Consumer Finances data from 1989–2016, that the median net worth of white families was seven times greater than the median net worth of black families.

spans.heading: Racial wealth gap
spans.text: A 2017 Urban Institute report quantified these impacts: among people whose parents did not attend college, those from high-wealth families were 26% more likely to attend at least two years of college than those from low-wealth families.

spans.heading: Explanations of the racial wealth gap
spans.text: Even among quantitative studies, the percentage of the racial wealth gap attributed to any one of these causes varies widely.

spans.heading: Explanations of the racial wealth gap
spans.text: Herring and Henderson found that structural factors explained more of the racial wealth gap than cultural factors, but that even if all factors between White and Black Americans were equal, the mean racial wealth gap would remain at around $155,000.

spans.heading: Explanations of the racial wealth gap
spans.text: Maury Gittleman and Edward Wolff, in a 2004 study that analyzed wealth accumulation over the period of a decade, found that once income is controlled, there is not a significant racial difference in savings.

spans.heading: Explanations of the racial wealth gap
spans.text: Instead, Gittleman and Wolff found that the racial wealth gap would decrease if Black Americans inherited and earned at similar levels to White Americans.

spans.heading: Explanations of the racial wealth gap
spans.text: In contrast, recent studies by Ashman & Neumuller and Aliprantis & Carroll took independent approaches but concluded that income disparities between racial groups, over time, formed the largest cause of the racial wealth gap.

spans.heading: American Opportunity Accounts Act
spans.text: In an examination of the American Opportunity Accounts Act, Morningstar determined that "Baby bonds would cut the racial wealth gap in half in terms of resources available per child at age 18".

spans.heading: Effect on the racial wealth gap
spans.text: Zewde's 2019 analysis, using data from the 2015 Panel Study of Income Dynamics, projects that baby bonds which are means-tested on the basis of family wealth would reduce the median racial wealth gap from a factor of 16 to a factor of 1.4.

spans.heading: Effect on the racial wealth gap
spans.text: Cassidy et al. cite critiques which take issue with Zewde's study design: the analysis used the median family wealth rather than the mean family wealth.

spans.heading: Effect on the racial wealth gap
spans.text: Cassidy et al. argue that using the median skews the data by excluding 97% of the wealth held by the top 50% of white families, while Zewde argues that her analysis is representative of the average person.

spans.heading: Effect on the racial wealth gap
spans.text: Furthermore, Cassidy et al. find that baby bonds would only increase the wealth held by black families from 9% of total white wealth to 23% of total white wealth.

spans.heading: Effect on the racial wealth gap
spans.text: According to The Takeaway, various studies show that the most effective way for the US government to reduce the African American wealth gap is to issue baby bonds.
